# The baseline corpus

This is the null hypothesis. Every rule copyme emits is a rule the model does
*not* already follow, and this corpus is how "already follow" is defined: a
feature within half a standard deviation of these numbers produces no rule,
because telling a model to do what it does anyway spends tokens and dilutes the
lines that matter.

`scripts/build_baseline.py` reads every `*.txt` file in this directory, splits
each on a line containing only `---`, computes the v2 feature set over each
passage, and writes the means and spreads to `src/copyme/data/baseline.json`.
Only numbers are written; no text from this corpus ships in the package.

## Status: measured

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | Generated responses to plain user questions |
| Model | `claude-sonnet-5` |
| Date | 2026-11-02 |
| Passages | 1,152 |
| Words | 391,398 |
| Generated by | `scripts/generate_baseline_corpus.py` |

This replaces a hand-written 20-passage corpus of about 4,000 words. The
difference matters more than the size suggests: the hand-written version was one
person's impression of how a model writes, and on several features it was simply
wrong. Its passages were single paragraphs, which gave `paragraph_sentences_median`
a large false salience for every author; the real default is 3.0 sentences per
paragraph, and most authors sit near it, so that rule now correctly suppresses.

## How it was generated, and why that way

**One ordinary question per passage.** Asking for several passages per call would
have been five times cheaper and would have turned the task into
list-generation, which has its own register. The answer to a plain question is
the thing being measured.

**No system prompt and no style instruction.** Nothing tells the model how to
write. The prompts name a subject and ask for prose.

**Truncated responses discarded, not trimmed.** A response cut off mid-sentence
would inflate the fragment rate and distort closing-sentence length, both of
which copyme renders rules from. Two responses were dropped for this.

**Prompts ask for prose, and that is a correction.** The first attempt used
reference-style questions — *"Can you explain X?"*, *"What are the common mistakes
with X?"* — and 17 of the first 20 responses came back as headings and bullet
lists, because that is genuinely the model's default shape for a reference
question. Filtering those out would have built a baseline of "model prose, given
that the model happened to write prose", which is a narrower thing than the
model's default. So the prompts changed instead, and which shapes survive was
measured with `--probe` rather than assumed: four shapes returned prose every
time, four about half the time, and four never did and were dropped.

The distinction is between **format** and **style**. Asking for paragraphs rather
than bullets fixes the format, because copyme's features are prose features and
a bulleted list has no paragraph shape to measure. Nothing says a word about how
to write those paragraphs. It also matches where the baseline is used: when a
copyme profile is in a prompt, the model has been asked to write continuous
prose in a person's voice, so "what would it do unprompted?" means "what prose
would it write".

449 of 1,601 responses (28%) were still rejected as mostly lists, from the four
conversational shapes.

## What converged and what did not

`scripts/build_baseline.py --check` compares each feature's spread over the first
half of the corpus against the second half. **21 of 36 features are within the 5%
tolerance, including every feature that drives a substantive rule:** sentence
length and its variation, paragraph length, contraction rate, conjunction
openers, commas per sentence, fragment rate, discourse markers and closing
sentence length. On the hand-written corpus, sentence-length median (28%),
variation (44%) and conjunction openers (56%) were all unconverged.

15 features remain above the tolerance, and they are the **near-zero-frequency**
ones — emoji at 0.11 per 1,000 words, exclamations at 0.06, ellipses at 0.16,
semicolons at 0.52 — plus `lowercase_start_rate`, which is a near-constant at
0.999. These are rare events with heavy tails: the spread is set by a handful of
outlier passages, so it is noisy in relative terms however large the corpus gets
within reason.

For rule suppression this is mostly benign in direction. Where the model's mean
is near zero and its spread small, an author who genuinely uses semicolons or
exclamations lands many spreads away, and the suppression decision is robust even
if the spread itself is 70% out. The case it is **not** robust for is an author
sitting close to the half-standard-deviation threshold on one of those features,
where the rule could go either way. The per-feature figures are recorded in
`src/copyme/data/baseline.json` under `stability.unstable_features`, so that can
be checked rather than guessed at.

## Refreshing it

The full procedure is in
[../../../docs/how-to/refresh-the-baseline.md](../../../docs/how-to/refresh-the-baseline.md).
In short: regenerate with `scripts/generate_baseline_corpus.py`, check with
`scripts/build_baseline.py --check`, write with `--bump`, then re-read the rules
on the golden samples, because a phrasing tuned against one baseline can read as
an overclaim against another.
